title: Nebraska sweats out slow start before pulling away from Ohio: How did Huskers’ new pieces fit?
content:
LINCOLN, Neb. — Nebraska sweated through slow starts to both halves Saturday in the season opener, pushing past Ohio 49-21.

In one of the hottest games ever played at Memorial Stadium, the temperature soared past 95 degrees, causing Nebraska fans to leave by the thousands at halftime with the Huskers ahead by 1 point. Nebraska went on to score three fourth-quarter touchdowns to open what was a one-possession contest early in the fourth quarter.

After an uneasy offseason in Lincoln and an unusually understated approach by coach Matt Rhule ahead of his fourth season at Nebraska, the Huskers stoked plenty of nerves with disjointed periods of play.

Some concern existed in August that Nebraska might lose its NCAA-record sellout streak. It survived, advancing to 411 consecutive games. And so did the Huskers, who first led midway through the second quarter but erased worries of a disastrous upset loss in the fourth.

Ultimately, the Nebraska debuts of quarterback Anthony Colandrea and defensive coordinator Rob Aurich ended on solid notes. As did the debut of freshman running back Jamal Rule, who finished with 169 total yards and three touchdowns in his first collegiate game.

Here’s what we took away:

He made plays. He missed plays. He took risks. Nebraska’s first-year quarterback, a transfer from UNLV, avoided turnovers on Saturday, though there was a moment or two of worry.

Largely, Colandrea appeared composed. In his 32nd career start, he completed 18 of 32 passes for 275 yards and three touchdowns.

Colandrea scored his first touchdown with the Huskers on a 13-yard scamper around the left end in the third quarter. He showed escapability, without the breakaway speed of recent running quarterbacks at Nebraska.

The tradeoff for the Huskers is that they’ve got a quarterback with moxie and excellent accuracy. His timing with the backs and receivers was on point. At times, he put too much mustard on throws, leading to drops.

One thing we only saw late, as the Ohio defense tired: Colandrea extending plays to create downfield opportunities. But when he mixed in that element in the fourth quarter, the Nebraska offense turned much more potent.

How does a team completely blow the first play of the season? Nebraska surrendered a 68-yard gain immediately after the opening kickoff as Ohio quarterback Nick Poulos hit Riley Neer on a wide-open post route, on the first play for Aurich, the new defensive coordinator.

Nebraska cornerback Jeremiah Charles, in his second career start — the first one two years ago, here against UCLA, did not go well for Charles — released Neer at the line of scrimmage. Poulos took advantage of the clear miscommunication in the secondary to hit Neer, who put a move on safety Jamir Conn and raced to the 7-yard line. Andrew Marshall chased down the receiver from his corner spot on the opposite side of the field.

Beyond the inconceivable mishap, the Huskers looked reactive and a step slow on defense for the entire first quarter.

Rhule preaches winning the middle four. The objective drives his desire to defer if the Huskers win the pregame coin toss. They did. And after a needless blindside block on Jacory Barney that wiped out a 57-yard touchdown reception by Nyziah Hunter inside the final two minutes of the first half, Nebraska emerged from the locker room in the third quarter, leading 14-13, and looked listless on offense.

Mekhi Nelson was hit for a 3-yard loss on the Huskers’ first play, then Colandrea’s second-down heave, under pressure from defensive end Ike Ackerman, failed to reach the line of scrimmage. A flag came out for intentional grounding, a loss of 18 yards to create a third-and-31 situation. It was Nebraska’s only three-and-out of the game.

Rule didn’t start. That job went to Isaiah Mozee, who ripped off a 25-yard gain off right tackle Gunnar Gottula on the first Nebraska play from scrimmage.

Rule didn’t play second at running back. That was the job of Mekhi Nelson, the most seasoned runner among a stable of inexperienced backs.

But Rule scored the first touchdown, on a 1-yard plunge to cap the opening drive. He scored the second touchdown, a 24-yard reception to give Nebraska its first lead in the second quarter.

Rule led the Huskers in both carries and yards, with 15 for 122. He added two catches for 47 yards. He’s the most natural runner of the trio, looking especially impressive and well-balanced on a 13-yard gain to pick up a fourth-and-1 dive in the third quarter.

Nelson rushed 10 times for 64 yards and showed value as a receiver with a 51-yard touchdown reception in the fourth quarter. Mozee carried six times for 31.

Total output for three: 31 rushes for 217 yards and four receptions for 112. They scored five touchdowns. The Huskers will take that.

Nebraska has no plans to replace All-American Emmett Johnson with one back. But Rule is the best bet to become a workhorse in Big Ten play.

What might have happened Saturday if Nebraska opened against a team that invested in its roster at a level close to the Huskers?

The Huskers are one of nine Power 4 teams that didn’t schedule a nonconference game against a P4 foe. This year marks the first time in modern Nebraska history — 2020 excluded — that it will not play a power-conference foe outside of its conference schedule.

There were too many new pieces on Saturday for the Huskers to look smooth. Rhule hired six assistant coaches and promoted three others into full-time spots during the offseason.

The Huskers have ground to make up to avoid reliving the woes of teams that experienced similar seismic change.

Bowling Green and North Dakota await before Nebraska attempts to match up against someone its own size.
